Mini project · Exploratory data analysis

COVID-19 in India

State-wise cases (30 Jan – 6 Aug 2020) and national vaccination (15 Jan 2021 – 12 Aug 2024). Load → Inspect → Clean → Explore → Visualise → Summarise.

1,964,536confirmed cases, 6 Aug 2020
40,699deaths
67.6%of cases recovered
54,392new cases a day (7-day avg, 6 Aug)
2.21 Bvaccine doses given by Aug 2024
92.7%of first-dose recipients fully vaccinated
Every number above is printed by the notebook cells below.

1. Load

Read both CSV files (downloaded into a data/ folder the first time). Death is read as text on purpose, because it holds a stray value we want to catch.

Code
files = {"covid_19_india.csv": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/imdevskp/covid-19-india-data/master/complete.csv",
         "owid_india_vaccinations.csv": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/owid/covid-19-data/master/public/data/vaccinations/country_data/India.csv"}
os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
for name, url in files.items():
    if not os.path.exists(f"data/{name}"):
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, f"data/{name}")

3. Clean

What we found and fixed

  1. Death had a stray '0#' (Puducherry, 24 May) -> turned into 0.
  2. 40 state labels for 35 states / UTs (Telangana spelled 3 ways, three Union Territory of ... duplicates) -> merged.
  3. New deaths is all zeros and New cases often disagrees with the totals -> daily numbers are recomputed from the cumulative counts.
  4. Four dates are missing and 17 Jul is a copy of 16 Jul -> filled by interpolation (steps below).
  5. A few cumulative counts fall from one day to the next -> forced to never decrease.
Code
covid.columns = ["date", "state", "lat", "lon", "confirmed", "deaths", "recovered", "new_cases", "new_deaths", "new_recovered"]
covid["date"]   = pd.to_datetime(covid["date"])
covid["deaths"] = pd.to_numeric(covid["deaths"].str.replace("#", "", regex=False))      # '0#' -> 0
covid["state"]  = covid["state"].replace({
    "Telengana": "Telangana", "Telangana***": "Telangana",
    "Union Territory of Chandigarh": "Chandigarh",
    "Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir": "Jammu and Kashmir",
    "Union Territory of Ladakh": "Ladakh"})
print("States / UTs now:", covid.state.nunique())
Output
States / UTs now: 35

Find the date problems: which days are missing, and which day shows no change at all in the national total (a copied row).

Code
days  = pd.date_range(covid.date.min(), covid.date.max())
total = covid.groupby("date")["confirmed"].sum()

print("Dates missing from the file:        ", [d.strftime("%d %b") for d in days.difference(total.index)])
print("Days the national total did not change:", [d.strftime("%d %b") for d in total[(total.diff() == 0) & (total > 1000)].index])
Output
Dates missing from the file:         ['26 Jun', '01 Jul', '04 Jul', '06 Jul']
Days the national total did not change: ['17 Jul']

Rebuild a complete date x state table, repair the gaps, and compute daily numbers from the cumulative counts.

Code
def table(col):                       # one row per calendar day, one column per state
    return covid.pivot(index="date", columns="state", values=col).reindex(days)

conf, deaths, rec = table("confirmed"), table("deaths"), table("recovered")
for t in (conf, deaths, rec):
    t.loc["2020-07-17"] = np.nan      # copied-forward day: treat as missing
conf, deaths, rec = [t.interpolate(limit_area="inside").ffill().fillna(0).round().cummax() for t in (conf, deaths, rec)]

daily  = conf.diff().fillna(conf).clip(lower=0)           # new cases per state per day
active = (conf - deaths - rec).clip(lower=0)

nat = pd.DataFrame({"confirmed": conf.sum(axis=1), "recovered": rec.sum(axis=1), "deaths": deaths.sum(axis=1),
                    "active": active.sum(axis=1), "new_cases": daily.sum(axis=1)})
nat["avg7"] = nat.new_cases.rolling(7).mean()
nat.tail(3).style.format("{:,.0f}").format_index("{:%d %b %Y}")
Output
  confirmed recovered deaths active new_cases avg7
04 Aug 2020 1,855,745 1,230,509 38,938 586,298 52,050 53,227
05 Aug 2020 1,908,254 1,282,215 39,795 586,244 52,509 53,798
06 Aug 2020 1,964,536 1,328,336 40,699 595,501 56,282 54,392

Vaccination data: add the missing days, fill the gaps, and compute doses per day.

Code
vacc = vacc.set_index("date")[["total_vaccinations", "people_vaccinated", "people_fully_vaccinated", "total_boosters"]]
vacc = vacc.reindex(pd.date_range(vacc.index.min(), vacc.index.max()))      # add the missing days
vacc.loc[:"2022-01-12", "total_boosters"] = 0                               # boosters began on 13 Jan 2022
vacc = vacc.interpolate().ffill().cummax()                                  # fill gaps; totals never fall

vacc["daily"] = vacc.total_vaccinations.diff().fillna(0).clip(lower=0)
vacc["avg7"]  = vacc.daily.rolling(7).mean()
print("Missing values left:", vacc.iloc[:, :4].isna().sum().sum())
vacc.tail(3).style.format("{:,.0f}").format_index("{:%d %b %Y}")
Output
Missing values left: 0

4.2 State by state (6 Aug 2020)

Death rate = deaths / confirmed cases. Recovery rate = recovered / confirmed cases.

Code
states = pd.DataFrame({"confirmed": conf.iloc[-1], "recovered": rec.iloc[-1], "deaths": deaths.iloc[-1], "active": active.iloc[-1]})
states["share_%"]    = states.confirmed / states.confirmed.sum() * 100
states["death_rate_%"] = states.deaths / states.confirmed * 100
states["recovery_%"] = states.recovered / states.confirmed * 100
states = states.sort_values("confirmed", ascending=False)

share = lambda k: states.confirmed.head(k).sum() / states.confirmed.sum()
print(f"Top 5 states hold {share(5):.1%} of all cases, the top 10 hold {share(10):.1%}\n")

big = states[states.confirmed >= 10_000]          # states with at least 10,000 cases
show = lambda col, n, largest, f: ", ".join(f"{s} ({v:{f}}%)" for s, v in (big[col].nlargest(n) if largest else big[col].nsmallest(n)).items())
print("Highest death rate:", show("death_rate_%", 3, True, ".2f"))
print("Lowest death rate: ", show("death_rate_%", 3, False, ".2f"))
print("Best recovery:     ", show("recovery_%", 3, True, ".1f"))
print("Slowest recovery:  ", show("recovery_%", 3, False, ".1f"))

(states.head(10).style
   .format("{:,.0f}", subset=["confirmed", "recovered", "deaths", "active"])
   .format("{:.1f}", subset=["share_%", "recovery_%"]).format("{:.2f}", subset=["death_rate_%"])
   .background_gradient(subset=["confirmed"], cmap="Blues").background_gradient(subset=["death_rate_%"], cmap="Oranges"))

4.4 A reporting spike to be careful with

On 17 Jun the national death count jumped. Which states added them?

Code
added = deaths.diff().loc["2020-06-17"]
print(f"Deaths added on 17 Jun: {added.sum():,.0f}  ->  {added.nlargest(3).astype(int).to_dict()}")
usual = deaths.sum(axis=1).diff().loc["2020-06-01":"2020-06-30"].drop(pd.Timestamp("2020-06-17")).mean()
print(f"The other June days averaged {usual:,.0f} deaths, so this was most likely a backlog added in one go, not a one-day surge.")
Output
Deaths added on 17 Jun: 2,003  ->  {'Maharashtra': 1409, 'Delhi': 437, 'Tamil Nadu': 49}
The other June days averaged 335 deaths, so this was most likely a backlog added in one go, not a one-day surge.

5. Visualise: 12 charts

The look is set once in the setup cell, so each chart is only a few lines.

Chart 1: Cumulative cases

Confirmed cases rise steeply from late May; recoveries follow behind them; deaths stay small by comparison.

Code
ax = nat[["confirmed", "recovered", "deaths"]].plot(color=[BLUE, GREEN, ORANGE], lw=2.5)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(short); ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.legend(["Confirmed", "Recovered", "Deaths"], loc="upper left")
ax.set_title("India's cumulative COVID-19 cases passed 1.96 million by 6 Aug 2020");
Output

Chart 2: Daily new cases

Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(nat.index, nat.new_cases, color=LIGHT, label="Daily new cases")
ax.plot(nat.index, nat.avg7, color=BLUE, lw=2.5, label="7-day average")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(short); ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.set_title("Daily cases grew from dozens in March to over 54,000 a day by 6 Aug");
Output

Chart 3: The 10 states with the most cases

Code
top = states.confirmed.head(10)[::-1]
ax = top.plot.barh(color=BLUE, width=0.65)
ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], labels=[f"{v/1e3:,.0f}K  ({v/states.confirmed.sum():.1%})" for v in top], padding=5)
ax.set_xlim(0, top.max() * 1.2); ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(short); ax.set_ylabel("")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False); ax.grid(axis="x")
ax.set_title("Ten states account for 82% of India's confirmed cases");

Chart 4: How cases ended (8 biggest states)

Blue = still active, green = recovered, orange = died (too thin to label).

Code
mix = states.head(8)[["active", "recovered", "deaths"]]
mix = mix.div(mix.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100
ax = mix[::-1].plot.barh(stacked=True, color=[BLUE, GREEN, ORANGE], width=0.65, edgecolor="white")
for c in ax.containers[:2]:
    ax.bar_label(c, fmt="%.0f%%", label_type="center", color="white", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_xlabel("% of confirmed cases"); ax.set_ylabel("")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False); ax.grid(axis="x")
ax.legend(ncol=3, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.15))
ax.set_title("Recovery rates ranged widely across the eight biggest state outbreaks");

top4 = states.index[:4]
ax = daily[top4].rolling(7).mean().loc["2020-04":].plot(lw=2.5, color=[BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN, "#eda100"])
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(short); ax.set_xlabel(""); ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.set_title("Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka hit record highs on 6 Aug");

Chart 8: Death rate and recovery rate over time

Two separate panels, because the two rates are on very different scales.

Code
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
(nat.deaths / nat.confirmed * 100).loc["2020-04-01":].plot(ax=a1, color=ORANGE, lw=2.5)
(nat.recovered / nat.confirmed * 100).loc["2020-04-01":].plot(ax=a2, color=GREEN, lw=2.5)
a1.set_title("Deaths as % of confirmed", fontsize=11); a1.set_ylim(0, None)
a2.set_title("Recovered as % of confirmed", fontsize=11); a2.set_ylim(0, 100)
for a in (a1, a2): a.set_xlabel("")
fig.suptitle("Death rate peaked in mid-June at 3.4%, then fell to 2.1% as recoveries rose to 68%", x=0.01, ha="left", fontweight="bold", fontsize=14)
fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.93]);

6. Summary of findings

COVID-19 (to 6 Aug 2020)

  • Fast growth. 1,964,536 confirmed, 1,328,336 recovered and 40,699 deaths. Cases passed 100,000 on 19 May and 1 million on 17 Jul. July alone produced 54.9% of all cases, and the 7-day average reached 54,392 a day on 6 Aug (doubling about every 21 days).
  • Concentrated. Five states held 62.1% of cases and ten held 82.1%; Maharashtra alone had 23.8%.
  • Hotspots moved. Delhi peaked in June and fell sharply afterwards. Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka surged in July, and with Maharashtra were at record daily highs on 6 Aug. Tamil Nadu's average had already started to fall.
  • Outcomes differed. The death rate (deaths / confirmed) was 2.07% nationally and the recovery rate 67.6%. Among states with 10,000+ cases, Gujarat (3.83%) and Maharashtra (3.52%) were highest; Assam (0.24%) and Kerala (0.32%) were lowest.
  • A misleading spike. The death rate peaked at 3.44% on 17 Jun because 2,003 deaths were added in one day (1,846 of them in Maharashtra and Delhi), most likely a backlog of earlier deaths.
  • Spread. Kerala reported the first case on 30 Jan; all 35 states / UTs had cases by 26 May.

Vaccination (Jan 2021 - Aug 2024)

  • Scale. 2.207 billion doses; 1.027 billion people with at least one dose; 952 million fully vaccinated (92.7% of first-dose recipients); 227 million booster doses.
  • Speed. 1 billion doses on 21 Oct 2021 (day 279) and 2 billion on 17 Jul 2022. The biggest day was 18.6 million doses (18 Sep 2021).
  • Front-loaded. 2021 delivered 1,449 million doses, 2022 delivered 752 million, and almost nothing is recorded after early 2023. That most likely means the data source stopped updating, not that vaccination stopped.

Limits to keep in mind

  • Counts are confirmed cases, which depend on how much testing was done.
  • There is no population data, so states cannot be compared per person (big states look worse in absolute terms).
  • August 2020 covers only 6 days, and the two datasets do not overlap in time, so no cause-and-effect link can be drawn between them.
  • Five days were filled by interpolation, so those daily figures are estimates.
Data: imdevskp/covid-19-india-data (MoHFW, covid19india.org) and Our World in Data. The two datasets cover different periods, so they are analysed side by side, not merged. To run it yourself: pip install pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn jupyter, then open the notebook and run all cells.
